name.text: When testing happens in a sprint

questiontext.text: In an agile sprint, when does testing take place?

answer.text: Continuously throughout the sprint, as each story is built

feedback.text: Correct — testing is woven through the whole sprint, not saved for the end.

answer.text: Only in a dedicated test phase during the last two days of the sprint

feedback.text: That end-loaded pattern is the mini-waterfall smell, not the agile cadence.

answer.text: Only after the sprint, in a separate testing sprint

feedback.text: A separate testing sprint is an anti-pattern; testing belongs inside each sprint.

answer.text: Only once the release is deployed to production

feedback.text: Waiting until production defeats the fast-feedback purpose of the sprint.

generalfeedback.text: Agile testing is continuous: each user story is developed and tested within the same sprint. Testing is an ongoing activity throughout the iteration, not a phase bolted on at the end.

questiontext.text: In agile, quality is a whole-team responsibility — testing is not solely the job of a separate QA department.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — the whole team owns quality; testing is a shared activity.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Agile treats quality as everyone's responsibility, not something delegated to a QA silo.

generalfeedback.text: A core agile principle is whole-team responsibility for quality: developers, testers, and the product owner all contribute to building and verifying the product. "Testing is the QA team's phase" is exactly the mindset agile moves away from.

questiontext.text: Which item most clearly belongs in a healthy Definition of Done for a user story?

answer.text: The story has been tested, automated where sensible, with no known critical defects

feedback.text: Correct — a proper DoD requires the story to be tested, not just coded.

answer.text: The code compiles and has been merged to the main branch

feedback.text: Compiling and merging is not enough; Done requires the story to be tested.

answer.text: The developer believes the code probably works

feedback.text: A belief is not verification; Done means the behaviour has actually been tested.

answer.text: Testing has been scheduled for a later hardening sprint

feedback.text: Deferring testing to a later sprint means the story is not Done now.

generalfeedback.text: The Definition of Done includes testing: a story counts as Done only when it has been tested (with automation where sensible) and carries no known critical defects. This keeps every increment trustworthy.

questiontext.text: Each sprint aims to produce a potentially shippable increment. What does that mean?

answer.text: A tested, working increment that could be released at the end of the sprint

feedback.text: Correct — potentially shippable means it is releasable in principle because quality is built in.

answer.text: A set of features that has been coded but not yet tested

feedback.text: Untested code is not potentially shippable; testing is part of what makes it releasable.

answer.text: A design document describing what will be built next sprint

feedback.text: An increment is working software, not a plan for future work.

answer.text: A prototype that must go through a separate QA sprint before release

feedback.text: Needing a later QA sprint means it was not shippable at sprint end.

generalfeedback.text: A potentially shippable increment is working, tested software that the organisation could choose to release. "Potentially" refers to a business decision, not to unfinished quality work — the testing must already be done within the sprint.

questiontext.text: In a healthy sprint cadence, when do testers first get involved with a user story?

answer.text: Early — during backlog refinement and sprint planning, helping shape acceptance criteria

feedback.text: Correct — testers engage early (shift-left) so quality is designed in from the start.

answer.text: Only after all coding for the story is finished

feedback.text: Waiting until coding is done delays feedback and is the pattern agile avoids.

answer.text: Only during the sprint review demo

feedback.text: The review is far too late for a tester to first engage with a story.

answer.text: Only in the next sprint, after development finishes this one

feedback.text: Testing a sprint behind development is an anti-pattern, not early engagement.

generalfeedback.text: Testers engage early — "shift-left" within the sprint. They join refinement and planning, help define acceptance criteria and concrete examples, and test each story as it is built rather than waiting for a batch at the end.

name.text: Develop and test within the same sprint

questiontext.text: For a user story to be considered Done, it should be both developed and tested within the same sprint.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — development and testing of a story happen in the same sprint so it can be Done.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Splitting development and testing across sprints breaks the cadence; both belong in the same sprint.

generalfeedback.text: Each story is developed and tested within one sprint. Only then does it meet a Definition of Done that includes testing and contribute to a potentially shippable increment.

questiontext.text: Which practice fits a healthy agile testing cadence?

answer.text: Testing each story as soon as it is built, rather than batching all testing at sprint end

feedback.text: Correct — testing stories as they complete keeps feedback fast and steady.

answer.text: Holding all testing until every story is code-complete

feedback.text: Batching testing to the end creates a crunch and delays feedback.

answer.text: Scheduling a hardening sprint to catch up on skipped testing

feedback.text: A hardening sprint signals that in-sprint testing was insufficient.

answer.text: Having developers hand finished code to QA for the next sprint

feedback.text: Testing a sprint behind development delays feedback and causes carryover.

generalfeedback.text: Testing each story as it is built keeps quality feedback flowing throughout the sprint. Batching, hardening sprints, and testing a sprint behind all break the cadence.

name.text: Meaning of shift-left in a sprint

questiontext.text: Within a sprint, shift-left testing means:

answer.text: Moving testing activities earlier — into planning and alongside development — rather than to the end

feedback.text: Correct — shift-left pulls testing thinking forward in the sprint.

answer.text: Moving testing to a specialised team after the sprint ends

feedback.text: That pushes testing later and outside the sprint, the opposite of shift-left.

answer.text: Testing only the left half of the user interface first

feedback.text: Shift-left is about timing in the workflow, not screen layout.

answer.text: Letting users test in production before the team does

feedback.text: That shifts testing right, to after release, not left.

generalfeedback.text: Shift-left means engaging testing earlier in the flow: helping define acceptance criteria in planning and refinement, pairing with developers, and testing each story as it is built. The goal is faster feedback and defects caught while cheap to fix.

name.text: Agile does not eliminate testing effort

questiontext.text: Because agile spreads testing throughout the sprint, the team no longer needs to spend any effort on testing.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Agile redistributes testing across the sprint; it does not remove the effort. Exploratory testing and acceptance testing still happen.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — testing effort is still real; it is woven through the sprint rather than eliminated.

generalfeedback.text: Agile changes when and how testing happens — continuous, whole-team, in-sprint — but the work does not vanish. Automation, exploratory testing, and acceptance testing all still require effort; they simply happen within the cadence instead of as a final phase.

questiontext.text: A team codes all stories first, then reserves a separate testing phase for the final days of the sprint. How should this be judged?

answer.text: An anti-pattern — a mini-waterfall inside the sprint that delays feedback

feedback.text: Correct — an end-loaded test phase is the mini-waterfall smell.

answer.text: A best practice, because testing is easier once everything is built

feedback.text: Batching testing to the end concentrates risk and delays feedback; it is not best practice.

answer.text: Required by Scrum, which mandates a test phase each sprint

feedback.text: Scrum mandates no such phase; it expects testing woven throughout.

answer.text: Fine, as long as the testers are a separate team

feedback.text: Handing off to a separate team late makes the delay and silo worse, not fine.

generalfeedback.text: Reserving testing for the end recreates a small waterfall inside the sprint. Defects surface late, when there is little time to fix them, and feedback to developers is delayed. Test each story as it is built instead.

questiontext.text: What is the main purpose of in-sprint test automation?

answer.text: To keep the growing regression suite runnable each sprint so feedback stays fast

feedback.text: Correct — automation lets the ever-larger regression run repeatedly and cheaply.

answer.text: To replace the need for any human judgement in testing

feedback.text: Automation complements exploratory and human testing; it does not replace it.

answer.text: To let the team skip writing a Definition of Done

feedback.text: Automation supports the DoD; it does not remove the need for one.

answer.text: To move all testing into a later hardening sprint

feedback.text: Automation exists precisely so testing stays in-sprint, not deferred.

generalfeedback.text: As sprints accumulate, the regression suite grows. Automating it in-sprint keeps that suite runnable every sprint, giving fast feedback and preventing manual regression from becoming an unsustainable end-of-sprint burden.

questiontext.text: Testers can contribute during backlog refinement by helping define clear acceptance criteria and concrete examples.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — testers help make stories testable and unambiguous during refinement.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Testers add value early: refinement is where they help sharpen acceptance criteria and examples.

generalfeedback.text: Testers engaging in refinement and planning helps surface edge cases and ambiguities before coding begins, producing testable stories with agreed acceptance criteria. This is a key part of shifting testing left within the cadence.

questiontext.text: In a Scrum team, who is responsible for the quality of the increment?

answer.text: The whole team — developers, testers, and product owner together

feedback.text: Correct — quality is a shared, whole-team responsibility.

answer.text: Only the testers, who form a gate before release

feedback.text: Making testers a gate recreates the QA silo agile avoids.

answer.text: Only the Scrum Master, who signs off each story

feedback.text: The Scrum Master facilitates; they do not own quality alone.

answer.text: Only the product owner, who accepts the increment

feedback.text: The product owner accepts value, but quality is built by the whole team.

generalfeedback.text: Quality is a whole-team responsibility. Everyone contributes to building it in and verifying it, rather than delegating it to a single role or a downstream gate.

questiontext.text: At the sprint review, what does the team demonstrate?

answer.text: A working, tested increment of the product

feedback.text: Correct — the review shows a real, tested increment, not unverified work.

answer.text: Untested code that still needs a later QA pass

feedback.text: Demonstrating untested work means the increment was not actually Done.

answer.text: Only slides describing what was planned

feedback.text: The review centres on working software, not planning slides.

answer.text: A list of defects to be tested next sprint

feedback.text: Deferring testing to next sprint is the cadence anti-pattern, not what a review presents.

generalfeedback.text: The sprint review demonstrates a working, tested increment — the outcome of development and testing done within the sprint. Because Done includes testing, what is shown is genuinely potentially shippable.

questiontext.text: A tester pairs with a developer to test a story as it is being built. Does this fit the agile testing cadence?

answer.text: Yes — testing as the story is built gives immediate feedback and keeps quality in-sprint

feedback.text: Correct — pairing while building is exactly the continuous, whole-team cadence.

answer.text: No — testers should never look at a story until it is fully code-complete

feedback.text: Waiting for code-complete delays feedback; early collaboration is preferred.

answer.text: No — testing must wait for a dedicated hardening sprint

feedback.text: Deferring to a hardening sprint is an anti-pattern, not the cadence.

answer.text: Only if the tester belongs to a separate QA department

feedback.text: Agile favours whole-team collaboration, not a separate QA gate.

generalfeedback.text: Pairing a tester with a developer while the story is built embodies whole-team quality and shift-left testing: defects are caught immediately and the story reaches Done within the sprint.

name.text: Why test each story as it is built

questiontext.text: Why is it better to test each story as it is built instead of batching all testing at the end of the sprint?

answer.text: Defects surface while the context is fresh and cheap to fix, and feedback reaches developers quickly

feedback.text: Correct — early, incremental testing shortens the feedback loop and lowers fix cost.

answer.text: It lets the team skip writing automated regression tests

feedback.text: Testing early does not remove the need for automation; the two work together.

answer.text: It guarantees that no defects will ever be found

feedback.text: No practice guarantees zero defects; the benefit is faster, cheaper feedback.

answer.text: It moves all responsibility for quality onto the testers

feedback.text: Agile spreads quality across the whole team; it does not concentrate it on testers.

generalfeedback.text: Testing a story as soon as it is built gives developers feedback while the code is fresh in mind, when defects are cheapest to fix. Batching to the end delays that feedback and concentrates risk in the final days.

questiontext.text: Which description best matches the mini-waterfall inside a sprint smell?

answer.text: The team codes all stories first, then crams every test activity into the last days of the sprint

feedback.text: Correct — an end-loaded test phase within the sprint is the mini-waterfall.

answer.text: The team writes acceptance criteria before any coding begins

feedback.text: Defining criteria up front is good shift-left practice, not the smell.

answer.text: The team automates its regression suite every sprint

feedback.text: In-sprint automation supports the cadence; it is not the smell.

answer.text: Developers and testers pair on each story as it is built

feedback.text: Pairing while building is exactly the healthy cadence, not the smell.

generalfeedback.text: The mini-waterfall recreates the phases of a waterfall project inside a single sprint: analyse, code, then test at the end. It delays feedback and produces an end-of-sprint crunch.

questiontext.text: A team suffers the mini-waterfall smell. What is the most appropriate fix?

answer.text: Test each story as soon as it is ready, with devs and testers collaborating throughout the sprint

feedback.text: Correct — spreading testing across the sprint removes the end-loaded crunch.

answer.text: Add a hardening sprint after every few sprints to catch up

feedback.text: A hardening sprint masks the problem instead of restoring the cadence.

answer.text: Push testing into the following sprint so coding can continue uninterrupted

feedback.text: Testing a sprint behind delays feedback and creates carryover.

answer.text: Hire a separate QA team to test after the sprint closes

feedback.text: A downstream QA gate reintroduces the silo and the delay.

generalfeedback.text: The fix is to flatten the waterfall: slice work so each story is tested as it becomes ready, with the whole team collaborating. This keeps feedback fast and the increment continuously close to Done.

questiontext.text: What is the core problem with a "throw it over the wall to QA" hand-off?

answer.text: It creates a hand-off delay and a quality silo, so defects are found late by people detached from the context

feedback.text: Correct — the hand-off delays feedback and separates quality from the team that built it.

answer.text: It makes testing too fast, so defects are missed

feedback.text: The problem is delay and detachment, not excessive speed.

answer.text: It forces developers to write acceptance criteria too early

feedback.text: Early criteria are helpful; that is not the hand-off problem.

answer.text: It removes the need for a Definition of Done

feedback.text: A hand-off model still needs a DoD; the issue is the silo and delay.

generalfeedback.text: Throwing work over the wall to a separate QA group breaks whole-team quality. Feedback arrives late, the testers lack the context of how the code was built, and defects pile up at the boundary rather than being caught continuously.

questiontext.text: Because the Definition of Done includes testing, how should a story that is coded but not yet tested at sprint end be treated?

answer.text: As not Done — it cannot be counted as complete or part of the shippable increment

feedback.text: Correct — untested work fails the DoD and is not Done.

answer.text: As Done, since the code exists and can be tested later

feedback.text: Existing code is not Done if the DoD requires testing that has not happened.

answer.text: As half Done, earning half its story points

feedback.text: Stories are binary against the DoD; there is no partial credit.

answer.text: As Done, provided a hardening sprint is planned

feedback.text: Planning later testing does not make an untested story Done now.

generalfeedback.text: If the DoD includes testing, an untested story is simply not Done. It is not counted toward velocity and does not belong in the shippable increment; the remaining testing carries over.

questiontext.text: What is the main benefit of involving testers during backlog refinement and planning?

answer.text: Ambiguities and edge cases are surfaced early, producing testable stories with agreed acceptance criteria

feedback.text: Correct — early tester input makes stories clearer and testable before coding.

answer.text: Developers can then skip writing any unit tests

feedback.text: Tester involvement in planning does not remove developer testing duties.

answer.text: The product owner no longer needs to prioritise the backlog

feedback.text: Prioritisation remains the product owner's job; refinement does not replace it.

answer.text: Testing can then be safely deferred to the next sprint

feedback.text: Early planning input is meant to keep testing in-sprint, not defer it.

generalfeedback.text: Testers thinking about a story during refinement and planning expose edge cases and ambiguities before code is written. The result is testable stories with clear, agreed acceptance criteria — fewer surprises and less rework later in the sprint.

questiontext.text: Why does sustainable agile testing rely on automating tests within each sprint?

answer.text: The regression suite grows every sprint; without automation, re-running it manually each sprint becomes unsustainable

feedback.text: Correct — automation keeps the growing regression affordable to run repeatedly.

answer.text: Automated tests never need to be maintained once written

feedback.text: Automated tests do need maintenance; that is not the rationale.

answer.text: Automation lets the team drop its Definition of Done

feedback.text: Automation supports the DoD rather than replacing it.

answer.text: Manual testing is always inferior and should be eliminated

feedback.text: Exploratory and manual testing remain valuable; automation targets repeatable regression.

generalfeedback.text: Every sprint adds behaviour that must keep working. Manually retesting an ever-larger regression each sprint quickly overwhelms the team, so repeatable checks are automated in-sprint to keep feedback fast and the cadence sustainable.

questiontext.text: A story is "code complete" but its testing is unfinished when the sprint ends. How does it affect velocity?

answer.text: It earns no velocity credit this sprint and carries over, because it is not Done

feedback.text: Correct — undone stories give no credit and carry into the next sprint.

answer.text: It earns full velocity credit because the code exists

feedback.text: Code existing is not Done; counting it inflates velocity.

answer.text: It earns partial credit proportional to how much testing remains

feedback.text: Velocity uses Done/not-Done, not partial credit.

answer.text: It boosts velocity because it will be finished quickly next sprint

feedback.text: Future finishing does not create current-sprint credit.

generalfeedback.text: Velocity counts only Done stories. Because testing is part of Done, a code-complete-but-untested story earns nothing this sprint and carries over. Counting it anyway inflates velocity and hides work still to do.

questiontext.text: Agreeing acceptance criteria and concrete examples before coding a story mainly helps because:

answer.text: It builds shared understanding of expected behaviour, so the story is built and tested against the same target

feedback.text: Correct — shared examples align development and testing before coding starts.

answer.text: It lets the team avoid running any tests later

feedback.text: Criteria guide testing; they do not replace running tests.

answer.text: It guarantees the story will need no changes once coding starts

feedback.text: Understanding can still evolve; the benefit is alignment, not immutability.

answer.text: It shifts all testing to the end of the sprint

feedback.text: Agreeing criteria early shifts testing thinking left, not to the end.

generalfeedback.text: Concrete acceptance criteria and examples give developers and testers a shared, unambiguous target. The story is built to meet those examples and tested against them, reducing rework and misunderstanding — a shift-left, whole-team practice.

questiontext.text: Why does aiming for a potentially shippable increment force testing to happen within the sprint?

answer.text: An increment can only be releasable if its quality is verified during the sprint, not deferred

feedback.text: Correct — releasability requires the testing to already be done in-sprint.

answer.text: Because Scrum forbids writing any automated tests

feedback.text: Scrum does not forbid automation; automation actually supports shippability.

answer.text: Because the product owner personally tests every story

feedback.text: The product owner accepts value; the whole team does the testing.

answer.text: Because testing is cheaper if left until after several sprints

feedback.text: Deferring testing raises cost and risk; it does not make increments shippable.

generalfeedback.text: "Potentially shippable" means the increment could be released at any time. That is only true if quality has been verified within the sprint. Deferring testing leaves unknown quality, so the increment is not actually shippable.

questiontext.text: How does pairing a tester with a developer during development affect the feedback loop?

answer.text: It shortens the loop — issues are raised and fixed immediately, reducing later rework

feedback.text: Correct — immediate collaboration catches issues before they compound.

answer.text: It lengthens the loop, because two people slow everything down

feedback.text: Pairing shortens feedback for testing; it does not lengthen the quality loop.

answer.text: It has no effect, since feedback only matters after release

feedback.text: In-sprint feedback is central to agile; it does not only matter after release.

answer.text: It defers all feedback to the sprint review

feedback.text: Pairing gives feedback continuously, not only at the review.

generalfeedback.text: Pairing collapses the distance between writing code and testing it: problems are spotted and corrected on the spot, while context is fresh, instead of being logged as defects to fix days later. This is the whole-team, shift-left cadence in action.

questiontext.text: Which observation is a telltale symptom that a team has a mini-waterfall inside its sprint?

answer.text: Testers are idle early in the sprint and overloaded in its final days

feedback.text: Correct — an idle-then-crunch pattern signals end-loaded testing.

answer.text: Testers and developers pair on stories from day one

feedback.text: Day-one collaboration is the healthy cadence, not a symptom of the smell.

answer.text: The regression suite is automated and runs every sprint

feedback.text: Automated regression is good practice, not a symptom of the smell.

answer.text: Acceptance criteria are agreed during refinement

feedback.text: Agreeing criteria early is shift-left practice, not a mini-waterfall symptom.

generalfeedback.text: A classic mini-waterfall symptom is uneven load: nothing to test early because coding is still in progress, then a crush of testing at the end. Smooth, continuous testing throughout the sprint is the healthy alternative.

name.text: Risk of batch-testing at sprint end

questiontext.text: What is the main risk of batching all testing into the final days of the sprint?

answer.text: Defects are found too late to fix within the sprint, forcing rushed fixes or carryover

feedback.text: Correct — late discovery leaves no room to fix, so work slips or is rushed.

answer.text: The team will finish every story earlier than planned

feedback.text: Batching testing tends to cause slippage, not early finishes.

answer.text: Automated tests become impossible to write

feedback.text: Batching does not make automation impossible; it just delays feedback.

answer.text: The product owner must attend the daily scrum

feedback.text: That is unrelated to when testing happens.

generalfeedback.text: When testing is squeezed into the last days, any defect it finds arrives with too little time to fix. The result is a crunch, rushed low-quality fixes, or stories carrying over unfinished into the next sprint.

name.text: We will add tests next sprint

questiontext.text: A developer says, "Let's mark it Done now and add the tests next sprint." What does this most directly undermine?

answer.text: The Definition of Done — it hides untested work as complete and accrues test debt

feedback.text: Correct — calling untested work Done breaks the DoD and builds up debt.

answer.text: The daily scrum, which becomes unnecessary

feedback.text: The daily scrum is unaffected by this decision.

answer.text: The product backlog ordering

feedback.text: Backlog ordering is a separate concern from marking untested work Done.

answer.text: Nothing — deferring tests one sprint is standard agile practice

feedback.text: Deferring tests a sprint is an anti-pattern, not standard practice.

generalfeedback.text: Marking untested work as Done violates a DoD that includes testing. It disguises incomplete work as finished, inflates velocity, and accumulates test debt that must be repaid later — usually at higher cost.

questiontext.text: Under whole-team quality, what should happen when a defect is found mid-sprint?

answer.text: The team collaborates to address it promptly, rather than treating it as only the testers' problem

feedback.text: Correct — whole-team quality means the team swarms the issue together.

answer.text: It is logged and left for the QA team to handle after the sprint

feedback.text: Leaving it for a downstream QA team recreates the silo and delay.

answer.text: It is ignored until the hardening sprint

feedback.text: Deferring to a hardening sprint lets the defect and debt linger.

answer.text: The tester who found it must fix it alone

feedback.text: Whole-team quality means shared ownership, not solo blame.

generalfeedback.text: With whole-team quality, a defect belongs to the team, not to whoever found it. The team swarms to fix it promptly so the story can reach Done within the sprint, keeping the increment shippable.

questiontext.text: A team's developers code throughout the sprint while testers only start testing in the final two days, when defects pile up. What is the diagnosis and remediation?

answer.text: Mini-waterfall inside the sprint; remediation is to test each story as it completes, with the whole team collaborating throughout

feedback.text: Correct — the end-loaded testing is a mini-waterfall, fixed by continuous in-sprint testing.

answer.text: Healthy cadence; no change needed because all testing still happens in-sprint

feedback.text: Being in-sprint is not enough; the end-loading is the problem.

answer.text: Testing-a-sprint-behind; remediation is to add a hardening sprint

feedback.text: This is not a sprint-behind pattern, and a hardening sprint would not fix it.

answer.text: A tooling problem; remediation is to buy a faster test runner

feedback.text: The issue is workflow timing, not test-runner speed.

generalfeedback.text: Coding first and testing last recreates a waterfall inside the sprint. The remedy is to flatten it: slice work so each story is testable soon, test it as it completes, and have developers and testers collaborate continuously so feedback is fast.

questiontext.text: Every third sprint, a team runs a dedicated hardening sprint to stabilise and test accumulated work. What does this indicate, and what is the fix?

answer.text: A smell of insufficient in-sprint testing and accumulating quality debt; the fix is to build quality in each sprint via a stronger DoD and in-sprint automation

feedback.text: Correct — a recurring hardening sprint signals debt that should be prevented in-sprint.

answer.text: A best practice that every mature agile team should adopt permanently

feedback.text: A permanent hardening sprint institutionalises the debt rather than removing it.

answer.text: Proof the team tests too much and should slow down

feedback.text: The problem is deferred testing, not excessive testing.

answer.text: A normal consequence of automating regression tests

feedback.text: Automation reduces the need for hardening; it does not cause it.

generalfeedback.text: A recurring hardening sprint is a symptom: quality work is being deferred and must be repaid in a catch-up sprint. The cure is to prevent the debt — a Definition of Done that includes testing, in-sprint automation, and continuous testing so each sprint's increment is already stable.

questiontext.text: Developers build features in sprint N, and testers test that same work in sprint N+1. What is the diagnosis and its main consequence?

answer.text: Testing lags a sprint behind development; feedback is delayed and untested work carries over, so "Done" is ambiguous

feedback.text: Correct — a one-sprint lag delays feedback and produces carryover and unclear Done.

answer.text: It is ideal pipelining that maximises throughput with no downside

feedback.text: The lag has real downsides: delayed feedback and carryover, not a free speed-up.

answer.text: A mini-waterfall confined to a single sprint

feedback.text: The lag spans two sprints; it is the sprint-behind anti-pattern, not a single-sprint mini-waterfall.

answer.text: Whole-team quality working as intended

feedback.text: Splitting build and test across sprints is the opposite of whole-team, in-sprint quality.

generalfeedback.text: When testing trails development by a sprint, defects in sprint N are not found until N+1 — after more work has been built on top. Feedback is delayed, stories carry over, and no sprint produces a genuinely Done increment. The remedy is to test within the same sprint.

questiontext.text: From a risk perspective, why must the Definition of Done require testing?

answer.text: Untested code has unknown quality, so calling it Done hides risk and lets debt accumulate silently

feedback.text: Correct — without testing, "Done" makes an unverified, risky claim.

answer.text: Testing is required only to satisfy an external auditor, not for risk

feedback.text: The reason is genuine quality risk, not merely audit compliance.

answer.text: Because testing makes the code run faster

feedback.text: Testing verifies behaviour; it is not primarily a performance optimisation.

answer.text: Because Scrum assigns testing to the product owner

feedback.text: Testing is a whole-team activity, and this is not why Done needs it.

generalfeedback.text: Done is a claim that the work is complete and trustworthy. Untested code carries unknown quality, so marking it Done conceals risk and quietly accrues debt. Requiring testing keeps Done honest and every increment potentially shippable.

questiontext.text: A team argues that deferring testing to sprint end lets them "code faster." What is the real trade-off?

answer.text: It feels faster short-term but raises defect cost, delays feedback, and risks an end-of-sprint crunch and carryover

feedback.text: Correct — the apparent speed is borrowed against later cost and risk.

answer.text: There is no trade-off; deferring testing is strictly faster overall

feedback.text: The later cost of late defects and carryover offsets the apparent speed.

answer.text: It slows coding immediately with no later benefit or cost

feedback.text: Deferral does not slow coding immediately; the cost lands later.

answer.text: It guarantees higher quality because tests run all at once

feedback.text: Running tests late tends to lower quality outcomes, not raise them.

generalfeedback.text: Deferring testing borrows apparent speed from the future: defects found late cost more to fix, feedback is delayed, and the sprint ends in a crunch with likely carryover. The short-term gain is repaid with interest.

questiontext.text: As sprints accumulate, how does a team keep the regression sustainable without lengthening the sprint?

answer.text: Automate regression checks in-sprint so the growing suite runs repeatedly and cheaply each sprint

feedback.text: Correct — in-sprint automation keeps the expanding regression affordable.

answer.text: Manually re-run the entire regression by hand every sprint

feedback.text: Manual re-runs grow without bound and become unsustainable.

answer.text: Stop testing older features once they have shipped once

feedback.text: Abandoning regression lets old features silently break.

answer.text: Batch all regression into an occasional hardening sprint

feedback.text: Batching regression into a hardening sprint delays feedback and hides debt.

generalfeedback.text: The regression suite grows with every sprint. Automating those repeatable checks in-sprint keeps the whole suite runnable each iteration, so feedback stays fast and the cadence holds without stretching the sprint or hiring endless manual testers.

questiontext.text: A team routinely marks code-complete stories as Done despite unfinished testing. What is the likely effect on velocity and carryover over time?

answer.text: Velocity looks inflated while hidden testing debt grows, eventually forcing carryover and a slowdown

feedback.text: Correct — counting undone work inflates velocity now and forces a reckoning later.

answer.text: Velocity becomes perfectly accurate and carryover disappears

feedback.text: Counting untested work makes velocity less accurate, not more.

answer.text: Velocity drops immediately with no hidden effects

feedback.text: The immediate effect is inflated velocity; the drop comes later.

answer.text: Carryover is eliminated because nothing is ever left undone

feedback.text: Testing is in fact left undone, so debt and carryover accumulate.

generalfeedback.text: Counting untested stories as Done inflates reported velocity while real testing debt piles up invisibly. When it must be repaid, the team slows down and stories carry over, making the earlier velocity figures misleading.

name.text: Testing sprint after several dev sprints

questiontext.text: A team plans several development-only sprints followed by one testing sprint. Why is this problematic and what is the better approach?

answer.text: It defers feedback and quality far downstream; better to test within every sprint so each yields a shippable increment

feedback.text: Correct — a separate testing sprint delays feedback; testing belongs in every sprint.

answer.text: It is fine, because concentrating testing improves focus

feedback.text: Concentrating testing downstream sacrifices fast feedback and shippability.

answer.text: It is required whenever the product is large

feedback.text: Product size does not justify separating testing into its own sprint.

answer.text: It is the same as pairing testers with developers

feedback.text: A separate testing sprint is the opposite of continuous, paired, in-sprint testing.

generalfeedback.text: A dedicated testing sprint pushes verification far from the code that created the risk, so defects are found late and no earlier sprint is truly Done. The better approach is to test within every sprint, keeping each increment potentially shippable.

name.text: Done story shipped a critical defect

questiontext.text: A story marked Done shipped a critical defect because "there was no time to test it." What was violated, and what is the remediation?

answer.text: The Definition of Done was violated; the fix is to enforce testing as part of Done and reduce work-in-progress so stories can be finished properly

feedback.text: Correct — the DoD was not met; enforce it and limit WIP so testing fits.

answer.text: Nothing was violated; shipping fast is more important than testing

feedback.text: Skipping testing violated the DoD and caused the escaped defect.

answer.text: The daily scrum was violated; the fix is longer stand-ups

feedback.text: The daily scrum is unrelated to skipping a story's testing.

answer.text: The backlog was violated; the fix is to add more stories

feedback.text: Adding stories worsens overload; it does not address the missing testing.

generalfeedback.text: Marking an untested story Done breaks a DoD that includes testing, and the escaped defect is the direct result. The remedy is to honour the DoD and to limit work-in-progress so the team can finish and test each story rather than overcommitting.

name.text: Remedy for a recurring end-of-sprint crunch

questiontext.text: A team keeps hitting an end-of-sprint testing crunch. Which change most directly restores a steady cadence?

answer.text: Limit work-in-progress and finish-and-test one story before pulling the next

feedback.text: Correct — limiting WIP and completing stories one at a time smooths testing across the sprint.

answer.text: Start every story at once so testing can all happen together at the end

feedback.text: Starting everything at once creates the end-loaded crunch, not a cure.

answer.text: Move all testing into the next sprint

feedback.text: Deferring to the next sprint is the sprint-behind anti-pattern.

answer.text: Extend the sprint length indefinitely

feedback.text: Longer sprints just enlarge the same crunch; they do not smooth the flow.

generalfeedback.text: An end-of-sprint crunch usually comes from too much work-in-progress finishing at once. Limiting WIP and completing (and testing) one story before starting the next spreads testing evenly across the sprint and keeps the increment close to Done throughout.

name.text: Automation does not remove exploratory testing

questiontext.text: Even with strong in-sprint automation, a team should still perform some exploratory and acceptance testing within the sprint.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — automation sustains regression, but human exploratory and acceptance testing remain valuable in-sprint.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Automation covers repeatable checks; it does not replace exploratory and acceptance testing.

generalfeedback.text: Automation is ideal for repeatable regression, keeping the growing suite runnable each sprint. But it does not replace human judgement: exploratory testing and user/acceptance testing still happen within the cadence. Agile weaves testing throughout; it does not eliminate its manual forms.

name.text: High velocity but rising escaped defects

questiontext.text: A team reports high velocity, yet escaped defects in production keep rising. What is the most likely cadence cause?

answer.text: Their Definition of Done omits real testing, so untested work is counted Done and defects slip through

feedback.text: Correct — a weak DoD lets untested work inflate velocity and leak defects.

answer.text: They are pairing testers with developers too early

feedback.text: Early pairing reduces escaped defects; it is not the cause.

answer.text: Their regression suite is too automated

feedback.text: More automation lowers escaped defects; over-automation is not the cause here.

answer.text: They hold a sprint retrospective every sprint

feedback.text: Retrospectives help improvement; they do not cause escaped defects.

generalfeedback.text: High velocity with rising escaped defects is a classic sign that "Done" does not really include testing. Work is marked complete before it is verified, so velocity looks good while defects leak to production. Strengthening the DoD to include testing realigns the numbers with reality.

name.text: Why hardening sprint is symptom not solution

questiontext.text: Why is a recurring hardening sprint best seen as a symptom rather than a solution?

answer.text: It reacts to accumulated debt after the fact instead of preventing it, and its recurring need signals a broken in-sprint cadence

feedback.text: Correct — it treats the symptom late rather than fixing the cadence that causes the debt.

answer.text: It is a solution, because it always eliminates the underlying debt permanently

feedback.text: It clears a backlog once but does nothing to stop the debt recurring.

answer.text: Because hardening sprints are forbidden by the Scrum Guide with penalties

feedback.text: The point is about cause and effect, not a formal prohibition or penalty.

answer.text: Because it makes the automated tests run more slowly

feedback.text: Test-runner speed is not why a hardening sprint is a symptom.

generalfeedback.text: A hardening sprint only cleans up debt that the regular sprints should not have created. If it is needed repeatedly, the real problem is upstream: testing is not happening within each sprint. Fixing the cadence removes the need for hardening.

questiontext.text: Each sprint, the count of stories developers call "done" far exceeds the count actually tested, and testers are perpetually overwhelmed. What is the diagnosis and fix?

answer.text: A work-in-progress imbalance creating a testing bottleneck; fix it with whole-team testing, limiting WIP, and swarming stories to Done

feedback.text: Correct — the gap is a WIP/bottleneck problem cured by shared testing and lower WIP.

answer.text: Testers are simply too slow and should be replaced

feedback.text: The issue is systemic WIP imbalance, not individual tester speed.

answer.text: Developers are too productive; they should write less code

feedback.text: The problem is unbalanced flow, not excess productivity; the answer is whole-team testing, not slowing coders.

answer.text: The Definition of Done should drop testing to close the gap

feedback.text: Dropping testing from Done hides the bottleneck and ships untested work.

generalfeedback.text: When developer "done" outruns tested work, quality is bottlenecked at testing. The cure is whole-team quality: developers help test, work-in-progress is limited, and the team swarms stories through to a Done that includes testing — not lowering the bar or blaming testers.

name.text: Feedback delay under a sprint lag

questiontext.text: When testing lags development by a full sprint, what happens to a defect introduced early in sprint N, and how should it be fixed?

answer.text: It is not found until sprint N+1, after more work is built on the faulty base; fix it by testing within the same sprint the code is written

feedback.text: Correct — the lag delays discovery until N+1, so remediation is to close the lag.

answer.text: It is found instantly, so the lag has no effect on feedback

feedback.text: A one-sprint lag delays discovery to N+1; it is not instant.

answer.text: It disappears on its own once the next sprint starts

feedback.text: Defects do not vanish; the lag merely postpones finding them.

answer.text: It is fixed by adding a hardening sprint after N+1

feedback.text: A hardening sprint compounds the delay rather than closing the lag.

generalfeedback.text: With testing a sprint behind, a defect from early in sprint N is not detected until sprint N+1, by which time further work has been built on the faulty base — making the fix larger and riskier. The remedy is to test the code within the same sprint it is written, closing the feedback gap.
